title: What your house doesn't hold
hookLine: true Master, what is there that is not in Your house (Anand, opening pauris)

lines: A KITCHEN THAT NEVER RUNS OUT.
cards: Some homes have a pantry that never seems to run out. A grandmother's kitchen where, no matter how many people turn up, there's always more: another pot of dal, another stack of rotis, a box of sweets from somewhere.
You arrive hungry and leave carrying leftovers, and you never once wonder whether there'll be enough.
Pauri three of Anand Sahib asks a question about a house like that, except the house is God's, and the question is almost a laugh of wonder.

teach.h: TRUE MASTER, WHAT ISN'T IN YOUR HOUSE?
teach.b: It opens, in the original: saachiaa saahibaa, kiaa naahee ghar terai. True Master, what isn't in your house? Then: everything is in your house.
A question that answers itself. The pauri says that whoever keeps your praise always, and holds your Name in their mind, finds the music of the Word playing within.
And it closes by asking again: says Nanak, true Master, what is not in your house? Two things make this more than a nice sentiment.

teach.h: GHAR: HOUSE, AND THE HOME WITHIN.
teach.b: First, ghar, house or home. In Sikh scripture, ghar often means more than a building: it's the inner home too, the self, the heart, where the Guru teaches the One is found. So the question works on two floors.
Nothing is missing from God's house. And, the pauri hints, nothing is missing from the house within you, if the Name is living there. Second, who this is for.
A lot of modern life runs on a quiet feeling of lack: not enough time, money, love, energy, success. Advertising depends on it.
Pauri three meets that feeling with a question, not a list of what to want: look around the house.
What isn't here? The pauri also says that each person receives what the Master gives; that line gets its own day soon. For today, just the wonder.

how: Many Sikhs recite this third pauri as part of the short Anand Sahib sung at the close of services, and its opening question is often quoted as an expression of trust and contentment.

o: in your house, where nothing is missing
a home you must earn by good deeds
the gurdwara, the house of worship

p: the music of the Word within

s: pauri three's opening is a question that answers itself
what is not in your house? everything is.
in Sikh scripture, ghar only ever means a building
it often means the inner home too: the heart, where the One is found.
the pauri tells the listener exactly what to want
it simply asks: what is missing? look around the house.

games.q: you're standing in the Master's house, worried there won't be enough. what does pauri three ask?
o: true Master, what is not in your house?
who else has more than me?
games.why: saachiaa saahibaa kiaa naahee ghar terai: true Master, what is not in your house? the question answers itself: everything is there.

practice: In your head, start a list of what's already in your house, and not just things: a roof, water from a tap, a person who'd answer if you called, your two hands, a memory you love.
Keep going until the list is a little longer than you expected. If you pray, you can say Waheguru after each one; if not, let the size of it sink in.

wordCard.voice: Ghar terai, in your house. Pauri three: true Master, what is not in your house? Everything is there, and the same may be true of the home within.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: ghar terai, in your house; pauri three asks what isn't there.

carryVoice: Your line: nothing is missing. It comes as a question, so it can be asked again. Day three hundred eighty-four, done.
